synopsis: Simulation credibility is an evidence-building process, not a tool feature: the checked frameworks require a defined use, risk-scaled effort, verification, physical-data validation, quantified uncertainty, independent review and a documented validity envelope [f5214, f7525]. On-road acceptance requires documented toolchain credibility and physical spot checks, but ISO 21815 does not explain how to establish credibility, and a 2026 preprint characterizes virtual-testing frameworks as “largely declarative” [f1214, f6928, f4411, f9455]. The ambition to provide confidence across all conditions and configurations faces substantial off-road gaps: no accepted sensor-model qualification method was found for dust, snow or fog, vendor sensor physics lacks independent weather validation, and photorealism alone does not establish validity [f31, f331, f8291, f3711]. Greater model complexity is not necessarily more accurate: a 2026 on-road round robin reported spreads of 0.033 seconds and 0.314 metres for more complex vehicle models, while point-mass models reproduced the prescribed profile exactly [f5907, f5908]. Credible capability took 42 months and 17 partners in PEGASUS and years in every other documented case; documented reductions in physical testing depended on earlier investment, a narrow operating envelope, or both, rather than a universal physical-test percentage [f60, f61, f59, f7534]. For a four-month heavy off-road validation, the recommended route is an analytical safety case, targeted physical tests and simulation under a credibility framework, with credibility evidence built before prototype arrival and no validated sensor-digital-twin claim before hardware and mounting are frozen and correlated [f2137, f11643, f11917].

Both make comparison against reality a prerequisite for credible model use.
